extracted.intended_audience: Practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents), disciplinary counsel, and adjudicators handling attorney-discipline matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria used in USPTO OED disciplinary proceedings to evaluate whether a patent practitioner violated the Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. pt. 10), including elements required to prove violations, duties to clients, and related contract/fraud defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to prove violation of 37 C.F.R. §§10.23(a),(b) via §10.23(c)(8)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether Respondent engaged in disreputable or gross misconduct in violation of 37 C.F.R. §§10.23(a) and (b) by violating Section 10.23(c)(8), the OED Director must prove by clear and convincing evidence that: (1) Mr. Openiano was Respondent’s client, (2) Respondent failed to inform him of correspondence received from the Office, (3) the correspondence was received by Respondent on behalf of Mr. Openiano, (4) the correspondence could have a significant effect on a matter pending before the Office, and (5) a reasonable practitioner would believe under the circumstances that Mr. Openiano should be notified of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision applies the five-element test to the facts (finding client relationship, identifying specific Office actions/Notices of Abandonment not communicated, showing those correspondences led to abandonment, and applying the reasonable-practitioner standard). Burden: clear and convincing evidence. Examples: non-final Office Actions, Notices of Abandonment, Notices to File Corrected Application Papers, Notices of Allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform client of Office correspondence that could significantly affect a matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must inform the client of correspondence received from the Office that could have a significant effect on a matter pending before the Office (e.g., non-final Office Actions, Notices to File Corrected Application Papers, Notices of Allowance, Notices of Abandonment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such notices provide requirements and deadlines to avoid abandonment; failure to notify deprives the client of the right to decide prosecution, and a reasonable practitioner would notify immediately because revival chances are higher if a petition is filed soon after abandonment. Examples/anti-patterns: withholding a Notice of Allowance or an Office Action because the attorney expects nonpayment is improper; failing to send copies or otherwise communicate deadlines is prejudicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to provide timely notice of abandonment and to advise about revival options
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must timely notify the client when an application becomes abandoned and provide the information necessary for the client to exercise rights to revive (including that revival requires showing the abandonment was unintentional and payment of petition and legal fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revival petitions require a showing that the delay was unintentional and payment of fees (e.g., filing fees of $850 or more plus legal fees to prepare the petition). Late notice reduces likelihood of successful revival and causes prejudice (client may not have funds/time to pursue revival). Example: notifying client one to four years after abandonment is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to comply with withdrawal procedures and provide due notice before ceasing work (37 C.F.R. §10.40)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner decides to stop providing legal services, he is required to seek permission to withdraw and to provide the client with due notice; attorneys do not have an absolute right to withdraw at any time without complying with applicable rules and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to seek withdrawal or to provide notice can constitute abandonment and subject the attorney to discipline. Case citations cited: Kirkland v. Golden Boy Promotions (attorneys must comply with rules and may be disciplined for withdrawing at a critical point); Atilus v. United States (attorney cannot bow out without notice and frustrate client's vital interests). Anti-pattern: simply 'stopping work' without informing client or the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of a matter entrusted to a practitioner (37 C.F.R. §10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner allowing patent applications to go abandoned without the client's consent or without appropriate action constitutes neglect of a matter entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic example: failing to file responses to Office Actions and Notices that result in abandonment. Evidence of neglect includes multiple instances of failing to respond across several applications; plausible alternative explanations (forgetfulness, busyness) must be weighed against evidence. Remedy: disciplinary finding under §10.77.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionally failing to seek lawful objectives of a client (37 C.F.R. §10.84(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner knowingly allowing patent applications to go abandoned, when the client seeks a patent and does not intend to abandon, can be found to have 'intentionally failed to seek the lawful objectives of a client through reasonably available means permitted by law and the Disciplinary Rules.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent's admission of intentionally not responding to Office notices supports this violation. Practitioner must pursue reasonably available means (e.g., filing responses, purchasing short extensions, advising client of options). Anti-pattern: intentionally failing to act because of anticipated nonpayment without advising the client or seeking withdrawal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional failure to carry out a contract of employment without withdrawing (37 C.F.R. §10.84(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to carry out a contract of employment entered into with a client for professional services, without properly withdrawing under the Rules, is a disciplinary violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely asserting lack of payment or a contract defense (e.g., under the UCC) does not excuse the duty to either perform or properly withdraw. Guidance: if attorney intends to void/avoid contract duties, must manifest that election to the client; otherwise disciplinary rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionally prejudicing or damaging a client during the professional relationship (37 C.F.R. §10.84(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally prejudicing or damaging a client by abandoning or failing to prosecute matters entrusted to the practitioner constitutes a violation (e.g., causing loss of ability to obtain or revive patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prejudice examples: lost chance to revive multiple patent applications, incurring substantial revival/legal costs, client inability to afford revival for multiple applications. Discipline may follow where abandonment causes tangible harm to client's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable-practitioner standard for notification and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether notification or other conduct was required is judged by what a reasonable practitioner would believe under the circumstances — e.g., whether a reasonable practitioner would have thought the client should be notified of a particular Office communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to facts: communications that state deadlines or requirements to avoid abandonment are ones a reasonable practitioner would notify the client about; the standard is objective and focuses on protecting client's right to decide prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and quality of evidence; credibility factors used in adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings require clear and convincing evidence; credibility determinations rely on consistency with prior statements, corroboration (e.g., notes/memos), witness demeanor (eye contact, composure), and the presence/absence of corroborating documentary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the judge credited Mr. Openiano due to consistency with his prior statements, contemporaneous notes, calm demeanor, and lack of contradictory evidence, while discounting Respondent's uncorroborated assertions. Anti-pattern: relying solely on self-serving testimony without documentary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense based on alleged fraudulent inducement — required elements to void contract
rubrics_metrics.description: If an attorney claims the attorney-client relationship was voided by the client's fraudulent inducement, the attorney must show elements of fraudulent inducement: (1) a misrepresentation; (2) that the client knew the representation was false and intended to induce entry into the contract; (3) actual reliance by the attorney on the misrepresentation; and (4) that reliance caused injury to the attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision cites Restatement §164 and case law; such a claim makes the contract voidable (not automatically nonexistent) and requires the party seeking to avoid duties to have expressed an election to do so. Anti-patterns: asserting fraud in conclusory fashion without particulars (courts disallow fraud claims that lack necessary detail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract-condition defenses must be specific and corroborated
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner cannot rely on an alleged condition in the contract (e.g., representation continues only if client pays) unless the condition is clearly established with specifics (when added, scope, amounts, which matters it applied to) and corroborating evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague, uncorroborated testimony that 'I told him representation would continue only if he paid' is insufficient. Best practice: obtain clear, written agreements modifying scope or suspending services, and effectuate withdrawal when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm significant client instructions in writing for serious matters (best practice/evidentiary expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable practitioner would confirm in writing decisions about abandoning a patent application or other serious changes in prosecution strategy; oral-only directions are insufficient to demonstrate client consent to abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision notes that where a client gave written instructions to pursue an application, the attorney should obtain written confirmation before treating the matter as abandoned. Failure to document such significant agreements undermines defenses that client consented to abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on withholding action or information because of nonpayment
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure of payment does not justify denying the client notice of Office actions or effectively stripping the client of the right to decide prosecution; attorneys cannot simply withhold notice or 'dun' a client for payment in lieu of providing required notifications/actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney conduct described as emailing the client to 'dun him for payment' and withholding notices was rejected; attorneys should instead follow withdrawal procedures or seek other remedies, not deprive clients of deadlines or notice.
